stories.headline: Winning, differently: On the by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry
stories.title: Winning, differently: On the by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry
stories.summary: Ruling parties sweep by-elections, but defections mar Tamil Nadu results
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: The by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, declared on Friday, held few surprises.
Barely five months after the April Assembly elections, the ruling party in each State/UT won all five bypolls.
What varied was the scale of victory.
In West Bengal, the BJP retained Nandigram and wrested Rejinagar, with strong vote shares of 76% and 63%.
In Puducherry, the ruling.
All India N.R. Congress also registered an emphatic win — 61% of the votes — in Thattanchavady.
Nandigram and Thattanchavady were vacated by the Chief Ministers, which partly explains the strong wins.
But the contests in Tamil Nadu were closer.
Dharapuram and Madurantakam fell vacant after their AIADMK MLAs resigned and defected to the ruling TVK, which renominated them.
Both won their seats back with 37% and 40% of the vote, respectively, leading the DMK rival candidates by about eight percentage points.
By-elections tend to favour the party in power, as voters prefer representatives with access to government.
But the variance between West Bengal and Tamil Nadu reflects the nature of contest in two similarly sized States but with vastly different political cultures.

stories.headline: SKUAST-K’s Green Campus Roadmap
stories.title: SKUAST-K’s Green Campus Roadmap
stories.summary: Climate change is no longer a far-off environmental concern confined to scientific discussions and policy documents. The Himalayan region of Kashmir stands at the centre of this emerging climate challenge. Extreme weather events have further intensified these problems. The devastating floods of 2014, which affected nearly 2.5 million people, claimed more than 280 lives, and caused estimated economic losses of around ₹1 lakh crore, remind us of Kashmir’s vulnerability to climate extremes. The unpredictability continues during 2026; J&K witnessed a marked increase in extreme rainfall events. According to the Director of the Meteorological Center, Kashmir, DrMukhtar Ahmad, 44 cloudbursts have struck Jammu and Kashmir since the onset of the monsoon this year, claiming about 35lives. These cloudburst incidents further triggered flash floods in Districts including Shopian, Anantnag, Bandipora and Budgam. The events have caused extensive damage to roads, bridges, homes and agricultural land, underscoring the region’s increasing vulnerability to climate-induced weather vagaries and the growing frequency of high-impact rainfall events. Universities as Climate Solution Hubs For a region where agriculture, horticulture, livestock, and natural resources sustain millions of livelihoods, climate resilience is now a necessity. In this backdrop, the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K) has developed and adopted its Green and Sustainable Campuses Policy, marking a paradigm shift from a conventional campus to a climate-smart institution. This Policy brings together the seven vast campuses, all research stations, and KrishiVigyanKendras (KVKs) to create a vibrant ecosystem that works towards resource-efficient, climate-smart, and low-carbon spaces, aligning itself with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Restoring Landscapes One of the major policy initiatives of SKUAST-K is its focus on restoring and reclaiming degraded landscapes and wastelands. The University has, on a massive scale, undertaken plantation, landscaping, and biodiversity enhancement initiatives across its campuses. Through cleaning drives, landscape development, and ecological rehabilitation, the neglected and degraded areas within university campuses have been systematically restored. The development of lawns, gardens, roadside landscapes, biodiversity spaces, and green recreational areas has transformed previously underutilized spaces into productive ecological assets. At its main campus in Shalimar, approximately 22,000 square feet of area has been converted into green lawn cover, along with the planting of 1,800 saplings of diverse species. These interventions have enhanced campus aesthetics and beautification besides aiding carbon sequestration, biodiversity enrichment, and improved microclimatic conditions. The university has extended its green restoration efforts past conventional landscaping. At the Faculty of Forestry in Benhama, Ganderbal, approximately 25,000 saplings have been planted on degraded southern hill slopes, including indigenous, arboreal, and selected exotic species, thereby supporting land restoration and biodiversity recovery. Similar plantation initiatives have also been undertaken at other campuses. Specialized biodiversity landscapes have also been developed, including Lavender and Rosemary Parks at the Faculty of Forestry, Benhama, which provide spaces for biodiversity conservation, experiential learning, and research. From Waste Management to Circular Agriculture A defining feature of SKUAST-K’s sustainability approach is its commitment to the circular economy—where waste is transformed into wealth. Across its campuses, research stations and extension centers, agricultural residues, crop waste, weeds and livestock manure are converted into compost and vermicompost, reducing dependence on chemical inputs while improving soil health. At the Shalimar campus, about 250 kg of kitchen waste is generated daily, which is then converted into nutrient-rich compost using mechanized composting units and used on university farms. Promoting the University’s vision of waste-to-wealth, the Mountain Livestock Research Institute produces approximately 200 tonnes of vermicompost annually, creating a sustainable model for a circular agricultural economy. The university is advancing conservation initiatives not only through landscape conservation reforms but also through a circular agri-economy. One of the university’s notable resource conservation initiatives involved refurbishing and repurposing old furniture rather than replacing it. The initiative resulted in savings of approximately ₹1.25 crore, reduced material waste, and freed over 4,000 square feet of storage space at the Shalimar campus—demonstrating that sustainability can also be economically efficient. Building Green Campuses Through Innovation To achieve its sustainability vision, the university is pursuing institutional transformation and has installed nearly 2,000 solar panels, 100 solar streetlights, and more than 15,000 LED bulbs across its campuses. Its paperless examination system alone saves approximately 22 lakh sheets of paper annually, equivalent to conserving around 264 trees, 44,000 liters of water, and notable energy resources. Digital governance initiatives, such as sustainability monitoring dashboards and paperless administrative processes, also demonstrate how technology can support environmental accountability. A Blueprint for Climate-Resilient Agriculture By embedding climate consciousness into governance, research, education, infrastructure, and extension, SKUAST-K is seriously pursuing the goal of sustaining tomorrow for future generations. Dr Nasir A Dar- Coordinator IQAC, SKUAST-K DrF.A.Lone- Head Environmental Science, SKUAST-K Dr Heeba Din, Editor,IQAC SKUAST-K

stories.headline: IHC, First Abu Dhabi eye stake in Bandhan Bank promoter
stories.title: IHC, First Abu Dhabi eye stake in Bandhan Bank promoter
stories.summary: Mumbai|Kolkata: IHC, the investment company of Abu Dhabi’s national security adviser and deputy ruler Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, is among those in early-stage discussions to buy into the promoter of Bandhan Bank, Bandhan Financial Services (BFSL), which owns a little more than a third of the private lender, said people aware of the development. The move is aimed at giving early stage financial investors an opportunity to sell stakes.ET was first to report in its March 13 edition that BFSL was looking to give its long term investors an exit.BFSL, led by Bandhan founder Chandra Shekhar Ghosh, has been working with advisers Jefferies to find strategic investors for 25-32%.134901881Up to $600m of StakeThat will open up an exit option for GIC of Singapore and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), backers of the firm for more than a decade. Together, these two held 30.3% of BFSL at the end of March, and have been seeking a full or partial exit, said the people cited. Their stake alone could be worth $500-600 million, they said.Other investors include Small Industries Development Bank of India (Sidbi), which owns 8.1%. Financial Inclusion Trust and North East Financial Inclusion Trust own a total 40.7%. The Bandhan Employees’ Welfare Trust holds 14.6%. If other shareholders also choose to exit, it will lead to a much larger transaction.Also read: Banks seek clarification on implementation of RBI forex measuresBFSL has two subsidiaries–Bandhan Technologies, an IT services and AI-led technology company, and Bandhan Financial Holdings, the holding company of Bandhan Bank, Bandhan AMC, Bandhan Mutual Fund Trustee, Bandhan Investment Managers (Mauritius) and Bandhan Life Insurance.As of March 31, BFSL owned 59.98% of Bandhan AMC and 97.16% of Bandhan Life Insurance Co. Singapore’s GIC and Chrys Capital are other investors in the asset management firm.Bandhan Financial Holdings Ltd had a stake of 37.5% in the bank at the end of June. As per the bank’s licensing agreement with the Reserve Bank of India, it must reduce the stake to 26% by 2030.Banks and sovereign funds have been widely canvassed in the Gulf for a stake in BFSL, said the people cited. They are said to include First Abu Dhabi Bank and Qatar Investment Authority as well as a few PE buyout funds such as Carlyle, EQT.“We don’t comment on market speculation,” Bandhan Bank chairman Ghosh told ET.A First Abu Dhabi Bank spokesperson said in reply to ET’s queries, “As a matter of policy, we do not comment on individual client relationships, transactions, or market speculation.”IHC and other entities cited above didn’t respond to queries.The discussions are at an early stage and there is no guarantee it will lead to a transaction, said the people cited.“Discussions are picking up momentum, but the contours are evolving,” said one investor who’s examining the deal. “It’s a complicated one and a lot depends on the regulator too.”Having started out as a microfinance lender in 2001, Bandhan became a full-fledged private sector bank in August 2015. It has one of the largest microfinance loan books in India--Rs 35,000 crore on June 30. The total loan book of the bank stands at Rs 1.56 lakh crore with total deposits of Rs 1.65 lakh crore. Bandhan has a capital adequacy ratio of 18.2% with common tier 1 ratio of 17.5% on June 30. The bank has 1,988 branches and a total customer base of 31.8 million.Also read: DBS Chief sees overseas confidence in India despite capital outflow concernsThe bank slashed its FY27 return on assets (RoA) guidance while announcing its June quarter results in July, triggering a 15% plunge in the stock to Rs 177.50, its sharpest intraday decline since the Covid-19 market crash in March 2020. On Monday, it ended at Rs 157, up 13.32% year to date, for a market value of Rs 25,351.40 crore.The guidance was driven primarily by external factors such as elevated technology cost and moderation in NIM outlook. Also, FY27 loan growth guidance was cut to the lower end of the 14-15% range guided earlier due to a slowdown owing to rising asset quality risk from higher energy costs and supply chain disruptions as well as uncertain monsoons.“Bandhan underscored that the growth cut was pre-emptive and that on the ground, asset-quality trends remain benign, including improving delinquency trends in both newer as well as older vintages, with the credit cost guidance retained at 1.6-1.8%,” said Anuj Singla and Harsh Wardhan Modi, analysts at JP Morgan. “Guidance cut was the key focus.”Gulf CorridorBandhan Technologies recently opened an office in Abu Dhabi. It also signed a strategic partnership in September 2026 with KMK Group, a subsidiary of the Khalid Al Hamed Group, in Abu Dhabi.Following the acquisition of RBL Bank by Emirates NBD, West Asian financial institutions have been actively scouting investment opportunities in lending and financial technology services firms. Emirates NBD completed its investment of $2.75 billion in RBL Bank in June after securing regulatory approvals, while IHC has committed $1 billion for a controlling stake in Sammaan Capital.“The UAE believes in India and is one of our largest foreign direct investment sources of capital. They have already invested $25 billion and are the seventh-largest source of FDI. They have also given intent to invest another $25 billion in the near future,” commerce and industry ministry Piyush Goyal said last month after co-chairing the 14th India-UAE High-Level Joint Task Force on Investments with Abu Dhabi Investment Authority Managing Director Sheikh Hamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.Goyal said the UAE aims to take its investments in India to $100 billion.

stories.headline: 6 Governors reassigned
stories.title: 6 Governors reassigned
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 12: Keralam Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar has been appointed as the Governor of Tamil Nadu, as part of a major gubernatorial reshuffle effected by President Droupadi Murmu on Monday. Om Prakash Mathur, Governor of Sikkim, will be the new Governor of Keralam in place of Arlekar, a communique issued by the Rashtrapati Bhavan said. Dushyant Gautam has been appointed the Governor of Sikkim, it said. Senior BJP leader from Jharkhand, Braj Mohan Ram, has been appointed as the Governor of Odisha. Sudha Yadav has been named the Governor of Karnataka and Dhal Singh Bisen will be Uttarakhand Governor, the communique said. These appointments will take effect from the dates they will assume charge of their respective offices, it said.

stories.headline: Dignity of asking questions restored
stories.title: Dignity of asking questions restored
stories.summary: Frankly speaking, I am not going to assess the performance of the Omar Abdullah government over the past two years. It is quite unfair to judge a government that is not even half as empowered as the governments I have seen since late 1970s. A government in Jammu and Kashmir was never a complete one, because it was always sought to be guided by forces other than those elected to govern. This has been true since the times of Sheikh Abdullah, even when he was regarded as the supreme leader and the state enjoyed the full autonomy that his descendants are yearning for today. Had the governments in J&K been given the authority to govern, Sheikh Abdullah would not have been deposed in 1953. Historians have the right to ask: if his government was dismissed for harbouring secessionist thoughts, why was he brought back to power? Congress owes this answer to the nation. Fast forward this to 2026: as Omar Abdullah the first Chief Minister of the Union Territory is about to complete two years in office in a couple of days, the complexities have multiplied. Today is the time to analyze things since October 8, 2024—the day the results of the Assembly polls made it clear that the National Conference, along with its allies, had won a majority of seats. Yet, it took eight days for his swearing-in ceremony. This is a rare period in the history of Jammu and Kashmir—not just because there are two overlapping centers of authority ordained by the UT status, but because of the kind of political, social, and cultural narratives it has engendered. It felt like a civilizational rebirth in Kashmir when people saw a reflection of their urges and aspirations in the government they voted to power. Notwithstanding the election results and the hyperbolic greetings offered to democracy in Jammu and Kashmir, the elected National Conference-Congress government has had to contend with an entrenched perception that the Abdullahs’ party represents a Kashmir-oriented political project. A lot of commentary, containing some very fair points, has been written and spoken by the opposition parties—the BJP in particular, though local opposition groups have been equally critical and harsh—in assessing the government’s performance and declaring it unsuccessful in delivering on its manifesto promises. The opposition has an inherent right in a democratic setup to assess and reassess the performance of the government, but the repeated questioning of the mandate itself goes against the established norms of a functioning democracy. The opposition could not have ignored the issues that concern the people. They challenged the government on everything from electricity supply to the regularization of daily wagers and jobs for the jobless. They pointed out the wide gaps between the manifesto promises and the actual reality on the ground. All the opposition groups, both within the legislature and outside of it, were on the same page regarding one thing: that the issue of statehood was a major distraction from day-to-day governance. And it is true that a common person worries more about daily issues than wider political ones—until they realize those broader issues are impinging on their land, individual and family dignity, and on a larger scale, the community and the whole territory. National Conference could not take its narrative to the grassroots level that the statehood was quite essential. Its leadership did speak of it but it could not convince the masses that it was not the party project but something what was historic and question of the day-to-day dignity of the people. There is no doubt that the local unit took upon itself to derail this project. The opposition deliberately ignored the actual reality and the way system operated without powers. This was way to distract attention from their own era of controlling the system. Daily governance issues are intrinsically linked to daily dignity. This dignity is common to all communities—Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, and Buddhists. It is the responsibility of the state to uphold this. There can be no separate dignity for different communities. To date, despite all his logical and persuasive arguments, Omar has not been able to secure statehood—his central mantra for improving governance within the system and on the ground. This is not entirely in his hands. The Centre has to go back to the drawing board and consider whether it is standing in the way of Omar Abdullah’s pursuit for the restoration of statehood, or if it has discovered new hurdles preventing the return of the status it had promised. There should be some clarity on this; if there is going to be further delay, it should be specified. That is what Omar is demanding to know. Since there are no specific answers, it raises a bigger question: is the elected government still being viewed through prism of old prejudices? In the context of Jammu and Kashmir, the question is not just political or administrative, but geopolitical and geostrategic. That requires a wider understanding of the situation and its requirements. In the current arrangement, accountability has become a one-way street. The elected government is held accountable for whatever goes wrong because it is the one meant to be questioned by the people. But things turn bizarre when voices start emerging from within the system itself, questioning the elected government over incidents that fall completely outside its jurisdiction. This undermines the real-time concept of accountability and stretches the elected government’s responsibility too far. Omar, as a politician, is not pleased with such criticism. He has built his own line of defense. At times, he brushes aside tough questions. Yet, what cannot be ignored is that he faces questions—and more often than not, he answers them. This dynamic has returned to Kashmir after a gap of many years. Today, questions are not formulated or prefaced with the vocabulary of flattery; they are tough. His answers provide a definitive perspective on critically important issues for the nation on the international stage, as well as for Jammu and Kashmir. opening: Frankly speaking, I am not going to assess the performance of the Omar Abdullah government over the past two years.
It is quite unfair to judge a government that is not even half as empowered as the governments.
body: I have seen since late 1970s.
A government in Jammu and Kashmir was never a complete one, because it was always sought to be guided by forces other than those elected to govern.
This has been true since the times of Sheikh Abdullah, even when he was regarded as the supreme leader and the state enjoyed the full autonomy that his descendants are yearning for today.
Had the governments in J&K been given the authority to govern, Sheikh Abdullah would not have been deposed in 1953.
Historians have the right to ask: if his government was dismissed for harbouring secessionist thoughts, why was he brought back to power?
Congress owes this answer to the nation.
Fast forward this to 2026: as Omar Abdullah the first Chief Minister of the Union Territory is about to complete two years in office in a couple of days, the complexities have multiplied.
Today is the time to analyze things since October 8, 2024—the day the results of the Assembly polls made it clear that the National Conference, along with its allies, had won a majority of seats.
Yet, it took eight days for his swearing-in ceremony.

This is a rare period in the history of Jammu and Kashmir—not just because there are two overlapping centers of authority ordained by the UT status, but because of the kind of political, social, and cultural narratives it has engendered.
It felt like a civilizational rebirth in Kashmir when people saw a reflection of their urges and aspirations in the government they voted to power.

Notwithstanding the election results and the hyperbolic greetings offered to democracy in Jammu and Kashmir, the elected National Conference-Congress government has had to contend with an entrenched perception that the Abdullahs’ party represents a Kashmir-oriented political project.

A lot of commentary, containing some very fair points, has been written and spoken by the opposition parties—the BJP in particular, though local opposition groups have been equally critical and harsh—in assessing the government’s performance and declaring it unsuccessful in delivering on its manifesto promises.

The opposition has an inherent right in a democratic setup to assess and reassess the performance of the government, but the repeated questioning of the mandate itself goes against the established norms of a functioning democracy.
The opposition could not have ignored the issues that concern the people.
They challenged the government on everything from electricity supply to the regularization of daily wagers and jobs for the jobless.
They pointed out the wide gaps between the manifesto promises and the actual reality on the ground.
All the opposition groups, both within the legislature and outside of it, were on the same page regarding one thing: that the issue of statehood was a major distraction from day-to-day governance.

And it is true that a common person worries more about daily issues than wider political ones—until they realize those broader issues are impinging on their land, individual and family dignity, and on a larger scale, the community and the whole territory.
National Conference could not take its narrative to the grassroots level that the statehood was quite essential.
Its leadership did speak of it but it could not convince the masses that it was not the party project but something what was historic and question of the day-to-day dignity of the people.
There is no doubt that the local unit took upon itself to derail this project.
The opposition deliberately ignored the actual reality and the way system operated without powers.
This was way to distract attention from their own era of controlling the system.
Daily governance issues are intrinsically linked to daily dignity.
This dignity is common to all communities—Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, and Buddhists.
It is the responsibility of the state to uphold this.
There can be no separate dignity for different communities.
To date, despite all his logical and persuasive arguments, Omar has not been able to secure statehood—his central mantra for improving governance within the system and on the ground.
This is not entirely in his hands.

The Centre has to go back to the drawing board and consider whether it is standing in the way of Omar Abdullah’s pursuit for the restoration of statehood, or if it has discovered new hurdles preventing the return of the status it had promised.
There should be some clarity on this; if there is going to be further delay, it should be specified.
That is what Omar is demanding to know.
Since there are no specific answers, it raises a bigger question: is the elected government still being viewed through prism of old prejudices?
In the context of Jammu and Kashmir, the question is not just political or administrative, but geopolitical and geostrategic.
That requires a wider understanding of the situation and its requirements.
In the current arrangement, accountability has become a one-way street.
The elected government is held accountable for whatever goes wrong because it is the one meant to be questioned by the people.
But things turn bizarre when voices start emerging from within the system itself, questioning the elected government over incidents that fall completely outside its jurisdiction.
This undermines the real-time concept of accountability and stretches the elected government’s responsibility too far.
Omar, as a politician, is not pleased with such criticism.
He has built his own line of defense.
At times, he brushes aside tough questions.
Yet, what cannot be ignored is that he faces questions—and more often than not, he answers them.
This dynamic has returned to Kashmir after a gap of many years.
Today, questions are not formulated or prefaced with the vocabulary of flattery; they are tough.
His answers provide a definitive perspective on critically important issues for the nation on the international stage, as well as for Jammu and Kashmir.
His willingness to encourage questions and face open-media-byte sessions on a daily basis has conferred a dignity to both the aspirations and the skepticism of ordinary people.

stories.headline: BJP urges INDIA alliance to put national interest above politics
stories.title: BJP urges INDIA alliance to put national interest above politics
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 12: Jammu and Kashmir BJP Chief Spokesperson and Senior Advocate Sunil Sethi on Monday urged the INDIA Alliance to prioritise national interest over political confrontation, stressing that democratic opposition must not compromise national security, institutional stability or public order. Sethi said every political party had the democratic right to oppose the government, question its policies and organise peaceful protests. However, he maintained that such opposition must be exercised responsibly and should not undermine public confidence in democratic institutions. Expressing concern over the growing politicisation of issues related to national security, constitutional institutions and India's international standing, Sethi said political parties must ensure that internal divisions and disagreements were not exploited by forces hostile to the country. He called upon the INDIA Alliance leadership to clarify its position on national security, public order and institutional stability amid political confrontations. “Opposition to a government is a democratic right, but safeguarding the nation is a responsibility shared by every political party,” Sethi said, adding that political differences must not compromise India's security, sovereignty or constitutional institutions. Sethi also said allegations of coordination between domestic political actors and forces hostile to India were serious matters that required credible evidence. Any instance of unlawful collaboration, foreign interference or incitement to violence, he added, should be investigated by the competent authorities in accordance with law. Emphasising the distinction between peaceful dissent and unlawful conduct, Sethi said democratic protests were constitutional rights, but violence, intimidation and deliberate disruption of public order could not be justified in the name of political opposition. He also questioned whether the INDIA Alliance was giving adequate attention to constructive policy alternatives on employment, economic development, public welfare and national security, arguing that political confrontation should not overshadow substantive public issues. Referring to Jammu and Kashmir, Sethi said the region's experience underlined the importance of public confidence, communal harmony and a clear distinction between democratic disagreement and activities that threaten national security. He urged political parties to exercise restraint while commenting on sensitive security matters and avoid statements that could deepen social divisions. “Governments will come and go, political alliances will change, and electoral contests will continue. But the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India must remain beyond partisan bargaining,” Sethi said. He called for a responsible political discourse that allows vigorous opposition and constitutional accountability while safeguarding national security and democratic freedoms.

article_sentences: The fund finances projects that support the reliability, security and stability of India's electricity grid.
It is mainly used to support investments important to secure power-system operations that may not be commercially viable for utilities.
The union budget for FY27 earmarked around ₹1,103 crore for the PSDF.
The ministry did not respond to an email seeking comment until press time Monday.
The Cabinet approval for the 15th finance commission cycle of FY22-26 period came in July 2023, with an allocation of ₹11,000 crore.

As per regulations, regional power committees, electricity generation companies, transmission licensees, distribution licensees, load dispatch centres and public sector undertakings need to give details of the projects and schemes for funding from the PSDF.

Categories eligible for funding include transmission systems of strategic importance, reactive energy generators, standard and special protection schemes, pilot and demonstration projects, and renovation and modernisation of transmission and distribution systems.
As India's renewable energy capacity increases, the grid needs additional voltage support, storage and protection systems to manage variable generation.

According to a Crisil Ratings report in March, addition of renewable energy capacity amid slower deployment of transmission infrastructure poses a risk of grid curtailment for more than 35 GW of capacity in fiscal 2027.
This is largely because of a lack of long-term grid access.
Curtailment for prolonged duration can impact the equity internal rate of return and the debt service coverage ratio of projects, the report said.
